(c) With \(d_k = 64\), a key that scores one standard deviation above three others gets unscaled scores \((8, 0, 0, 0)\). Compute \(\alpha_1\) and \(\partial \alpha_1 / \partial e_1 = \alpha_1(1 - \alpha_1)\), then repeat with the scaled scores \((1, 0, 0, 0)\).

(d) Why not divide by \(d_k\) instead, to be safe?

Hint

Write \(q^\top k = \sum_j q_j k_j\). The terms are independent with \(E[q_j k_j] = E[q_j]E[k_j]\) and \(E[q_j^2 k_j^2] = E[q_j^2]E[k_j^2]\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Each term has \(E[q_j k_j] = E[q_j]\,E[k_j] = 0\), so \(E[q^\top k] = 0\). Each term's variance is

\[ \operatorname{Var}(q_j k_j) = E[q_j^2 k_j^2] - 0 = E[q_j^2]\,E[k_j^2] = 1, \]

and because the \(d_k\) terms are independent their variances add: \(\operatorname{Var}(q^\top k) = d_k\), so the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{d_k}\).

(b) \(\operatorname{Var}\big(q^\top k / \sqrt{d_k}\big) = d_k / d_k = \mathbf{1}\).

(c) Unscaled:

\[ \alpha_1 = \frac{e^8}{e^8 + 3} = \mathbf{0.9990}, \qquad \alpha_1(1 - \alpha_1) = \mathbf{0.0010} \]

Scaled:

\[ \alpha_1 = \frac{e}{e + 3} = \mathbf{0.4754}, \qquad \alpha_1(1 - \alpha_1) = \mathbf{0.2494} \]

A typical one-standard-deviation gap makes the unscaled softmax essentially one-hot, and the gradient through it is about 250 times smaller.

(d) Dividing by \(d_k\) gives variance \(1 / d_k\), which shrinks with dimension: for \(d_k = 512\) all scores would be nearly equal and attention would collapse towards uniform averaging, losing the ability to select. \(\sqrt{d_k}\) is exactly the factor that keeps the variance at 1.

Key insight: Dot products of random vectors grow like \(\sqrt{d_k}\) in size; without the scaling, wider models would have saturated softmaxes and vanishing attention gradients from the start of training.

9.D Bahdanau Attention for Seq2seq (8.4)

P8.13 L1 · Foundation

The five-step Bahdanau pipeline

(a) Put these decoder-step equations in the order they are computed at step \(t\):

  • (i) \(c_t = \sum_{i=1}^{T} \alpha_{t,i} h_i\)
  • (ii) \(P(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x) = \operatorname{softmax}(W_o [s_t; c_t])\)
  • (iii) \(e_{t,i} = v^\top \tanh(W_s s_{t-1} + W_h h_i)\)
  • (iv) \(s_t = \operatorname{RNN}([y_{t-1}; c_t],\ s_{t-1})\)
  • (v) \(\alpha_{t,i} = \exp(e_{t,i}) / \sum_{j} \exp(e_{t,j})\)

(b) Why does the score use \(s_{t-1}\) rather than \(s_t\)?

(c) The encoder is a bidirectional RNN with 256 units in each direction. What is the size of each \(h_i\), and what does it summarise?

(d) True or false: "In Bahdanau attention the context vector is computed once per source sentence."

(e) In the query–key–value language, what plays the role of the query, the keys and the values?

Hint

The context has to be ready before the decoder state can be updated, because \(c_t\) is part of the RNN's input.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) (iii) align → (v) normalise → (i) context → (iv) update the decoder state → (ii) output distribution.

(b) \(s_t\) depends on \(c_t\) through equation (iv), so it does not exist yet when the scores are needed. The previous state \(s_{t-1}\) summarises everything generated so far and is the natural "what do I need next" query.

(c) \(h_i = [\overrightarrow{h}_i; \overleftarrow{h}_i]\) has 512 entries. It summarises the words before position \(i\) (forward pass) and after it (backward pass), centred on word \(i\).

(d) False. A fresh \(c_t\) is computed at every decoder step; that is the whole point compared with the fixed \(c\) of plain seq2seq.

(e) Query \(= s_{t-1}\); keys = values = the encoder states \(h_i\). Bahdanau attention is the original cross-attention.

Key insight: Bahdanau attention inserts "look back at all encoder states" between the decoder's previous state and its next state, so every output word gets its own context.

P8.14 L2 · Computation

Sizing a Bahdanau model and reading its alignments

A Hindi-to-English model has a bidirectional GRU encoder with 256 units per direction, a decoder state \(s_t\) of size 512, an attention hidden size of 256, word embeddings of size 300 and an English vocabulary of 10,000 words.

(a) Give the shapes of \(W_s\), \(W_h\) and \(v\) in \(e_{t,i} = v^\top \tanh(W_s s_{t-1} + W_h h_i)\), and the total number of attention parameters.

(b) What is the size of the decoder RNN input \([y_{t-1}; c_t]\)?

(c) How many weights and biases does the output layer \(\operatorname{softmax}(W_o [s_t; c_t] + b_o)\) have?

(d) For the source "main ghar ja raha hoon" (5 words) and the output "I am going home" (4 words), how many scores \(e_{t,i}\) are computed? The alignment matrix below has one entry missing in each row. Fill them in, and say what the pattern shows about word order.

target \(\backslash\) source main ghar ja raha hoon
I 0.80 0.05 0.04 0.03 ?
am 0.10 0.02 0.08 0.35 ?
going 0.03 0.10 ? 0.15 0.02
home 0.05 ? 0.10 0.03 0.02
Hint

\(h_i\) has size \(2 \times 256\). Each row of the alignment matrix is a softmax over source positions.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(W_s \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 512}\), \(W_h \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 512}\), \(v \in \mathbb{R}^{256}\), giving

\[ 131{,}072 + 131{,}072 + 256 = \mathbf{262{,}400} \]

attention parameters.

(b) \(300 + 512 =\) 812.

(c) \([s_t; c_t]\) has \(512 + 512 = 1024\) entries, so \(W_o\) is \(10{,}000 \times 1024\): 10,240,000 weights plus 10,000 biases = 10,250,000.

(d) \(T' \times T = 4 \times 5 = 20\) scores. Each row must sum to 1, so the missing entries are 0.08 (I–hoon), 0.45 (am–hoon), 0.70 (going–ja), 0.80 (home–ghar). The alignment is not diagonal: Hindi puts the object "ghar" before the verb, English puts "home" last, and attention simply looks back to position 2 when generating the last English word. "am" spreads its weight over "raha" and "hoon", the two words that carry tense.

Key insight: Attention adds relatively few parameters (the output layer dwarfs it), costs \(O(T T')\) scores per sentence, and learns alignments that can reorder freely, which a fixed context vector could never expose.

P8.15 L3 · Application

One full Bahdanau decoder step

A tiny model has a bidirectional encoder with one unit per direction, so each \(h_i \in \mathbb{R}^2\):

\[ h_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 \\ -0.2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad h_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 \\ 0.4 \end{pmatrix}, \quad h_3 = \begin{pmatrix} -0.3 \\ 0.8 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad s_{t-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.2 \\ -0.5 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Attention uses

\[ W_s = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad W_h = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0.5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad v = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

The decoder update is \(s_t = \tanh\big(A [y_{t-1}; c_t] + B s_{t-1}\big)\), where the previous word has a 1-dimensional embedding \(y_{t-1} = 0.5\), and the output layer is \(\operatorname{softmax}(W_o [s_t; c_t])\) over the vocabulary ("this", "book", "is"):

\[ A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad W_o = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \]

(a) Compute the alignment scores \(e_{t,1}, e_{t,2}, e_{t,3}\).

(b) Compute the attention weights and the context \(c_t\).

(c) Compute the new decoder state \(s_t\).

(d) Compute the output distribution, and the cross-entropy loss if the correct word is "book".

Hint

\(W_s s_{t-1} = (0.2, -0.5)^\top\) is shared by all three scores. With \(v = (1, 1)\), each score is the sum of the two tanh entries.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(W_h h_1 = (0.7, 0.05)\), \(W_h h_2 = (0.5, 0.85)\), \(W_h h_3 = (-1.1, 0.65)\). Adding \(W_s s_{t-1}\) gives \((0.9, -0.45)\), \((0.7, 0.35)\), \((-0.9, 0.15)\). Then

\[ e_{t,1} = 0.7163 - 0.4219 = \mathbf{0.2944}, \quad e_{t,2} = 0.6044 + 0.3364 = \mathbf{0.9407}, \quad e_{t,3} = -0.7163 + 0.1489 = \mathbf{-0.5674} \]

(b)

\[ \alpha_t = (\mathbf{0.3002},\ \mathbf{0.5730},\ \mathbf{0.1268}), \qquad c_t = \sum_i \alpha_{t,i} h_i = (\mathbf{0.6277},\ \mathbf{0.2706})^\top \]

(c) The RNN input is \([0.5;\ 0.6277;\ 0.2706]\). Then \(A[y_{t-1}; c_t] = (0.8139,\ 0.4924)\) and \(B s_{t-1} = (0.1,\ -0.25)\), so

\[ s_t = \tanh(0.9139,\ 0.2424) = (\mathbf{0.7230},\ \mathbf{0.2378})^\top \]

(d) \([s_t; c_t] = (0.7230, 0.2378, 0.6277, 0.2706)\) and \(W_o [s_t; c_t] = (1.3507,\ 0.5084,\ -0.4852)\), so

\[ P = (\mathbf{0.629},\ \mathbf{0.271},\ \mathbf{0.100}) \text{ for (this, book, is)}, \qquad L = -\ln 0.2709 = \mathbf{1.306} \]

The model currently prefers "this"; the gradient of \(L\) will flow back through \(W_o\), the RNN and the attention weights into \(W_s\), \(W_h\) and \(v\).

Key insight: Every decoder step runs align → normalise → context → update → predict, and the context enters twice: as an input to the RNN and directly into the output layer.

9.E Self, Cross, Masked & Multi-head Attention (8.5)

P8.16 L1 · Foundation

Where do Q, K and V come from?

(a) For each attention type, say where the queries come from, where the keys and values come from, and whether a causal mask is applied:

  • (i) self-attention in a translation encoder;
  • (ii) masked self-attention in a translation decoder;
  • (iii) cross-attention in a translation decoder;
  • (iv) attention in Bahdanau's RNN seq2seq model.

(b) A sequence of \(n\) tokens uses self-attention. What is the shape of the weight matrix? For cross-attention from \(m\) decoder tokens to \(n\) encoder tokens, what is it?

(c) True or false: "Multi-head attention is a fourth source of queries, alongside self, cross and masked."

(d) True or false: "A causal mask sets the weights of future positions to 0 by adding 0 to their scores."

Hint

The type of attention is decided by which sequence produces \(Q\) and which produces \(K, V\). Multi-head is about how many attention computations run in parallel, not where the inputs come from.

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

queries from keys/values from causal mask
(i) encoder self source tokens source tokens no
(ii) decoder masked self target tokens so far target tokens so far yes
(iii) decoder cross target tokens (decoder) encoder outputs no
(iv) Bahdanau decoder state \(s_{t-1}\) encoder states \(h_i\) no (it is cross-attention)

(b) \(n \times n\) for self-attention; \(m \times n\) for cross-attention (one row per query, one column per key).

(c) False. Multi-head runs \(h\) attention operations in parallel with different projections; each head can itself be self, cross or masked attention.

(d) False. The mask adds \(-\infty\) to the future scores, so \(e^{-\infty} = 0\) after the softmax. Adding 0 would change nothing.

Key insight: Self, cross and masked attention are the same formula; they differ only in where Q, K, V come from and which query–key pairs are allowed.

P8.17 L2 · Computation

Multi-head attention: shapes and parameters

A multi-head attention layer has \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\) and \(h = 8\) heads, with \(\operatorname{head}_i = \operatorname{Attention}(X W_i^Q, X W_i^K, X W_i^V)\) and output \(\operatorname{Concat}(\operatorname{head}_1, \dots, \operatorname{head}_8) W^O\). The input is a sentence of \(n = 10\) tokens.

(a) What are \(d_k\) and \(d_v\) per head?

(b) Give the shapes of \(X\), \(W_i^Q\), \(Q_i = X W_i^Q\), \(Q_i K_i^\top\), \(\operatorname{head}_i\), the concatenation, \(W^O\) and the layer output.

(c) Count the parameters of the layer, without and with biases on every projection.

(d) How many attention weights (entries of all the softmax matrices) does the layer compute for this sentence?

(e) Repeat (a) and (c) for a BERT-base layer with \(d_{\text{model}} = 768\), \(h = 12\), no biases.

Hint

With \(d_k = d_{\text{model}}/h\), the eight \(W_i^Q\) together form one \(512 \times 512\) matrix.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(d_k = d_v = 512 / 8 = 64\).

(b)

object shape
\(X\) \(10 \times 512\)
\(W_i^Q\) (also \(W_i^K, W_i^V\)) \(512 \times 64\)
\(Q_i\) (also \(K_i, V_i\)) \(10 \times 64\)
\(Q_i K_i^\top\) \(10 \times 10\)
\(\operatorname{head}_i\) \(10 \times 64\)
concatenation \(10 \times 512\)
\(W^O\) \(512 \times 512\)
output \(10 \times 512\)

(c) The query, key and value projections contribute \(3 \times 8 \times 512 \times 64 = 3 \times 512^2\), and \(W^O\) adds \(512^2\):

\[ 4 \times 512^2 = \mathbf{1{,}048{,}576} \text{ weights}, \qquad 1{,}048{,}576 + 4 \times 512 = \mathbf{1{,}050{,}624} \text{ with biases} \]

(d) Each head has a \(10 \times 10\) matrix: \(8 \times 100 =\) 800 weights.

(e) \(d_k = 768/12 = 64\) and \(4 \times 768^2 =\) 2,359,296 parameters.

Key insight: Splitting \(d_{\text{model}}\) into \(h\) heads of size \(d_{\text{model}}/h\) leaves the parameter count at \(4 d_{\text{model}}^2\) regardless of \(h\); heads change how the capacity is organised, not how much there is.

P8.18 L2 · Computation

Cross-attention from a decoder to an encoder

A decoder has two target tokens whose (already projected) queries are the rows of \(Q\), and the encoder has three source tokens with keys \(K\) and values \(V\) (\(d_k = 2\)):

\[ Q = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad K = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad V = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. \]

(a) Compute \(Q K^\top / \sqrt{d_k}\) and state its shape.

(b) Compute the weight matrix and the output \(\operatorname{softmax}(Q K^\top / \sqrt{d_k}) V\).

(c) Should a causal mask be applied here? Explain.

(d) The encoder batch is padded with a fourth token whose key and value are both \((0, 0)\). If no padding mask is used, recompute the first output row and say what went wrong.

Hint

\(\sqrt{2} = 1.4142\). For (d), a zero key still gets score 0, and \(e^0 = 1\) is not negligible.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Shape \(2 \times 3\) (queries by keys):

\[ \frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{2}} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.4142 & 0 & 1.4142 \\ 0 & 1.4142 & 1.4142 \end{pmatrix} \]

(b)

\[ A = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{0.4458} & \mathbf{0.1084} & \mathbf{0.4458} \\ \mathbf{0.1084} & \mathbf{0.4458} & \mathbf{0.4458} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad A V = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{2.675} & \mathbf{1.325} \\ \mathbf{1.325} & \mathbf{2.675} \end{pmatrix} \]

(c) No. The whole source sentence is available before decoding starts, so a decoder token may look at any encoder position. Causality is enforced in the decoder's own self-attention, not in cross-attention.

(d) The pad key gets score 0, so the first row of weights becomes \((0.4022,\ 0.0978,\ 0.4022,\ 0.0978)\) and the output row becomes \((2.413,\ 1.196)\) instead of \((2.675, 1.325)\). Almost 10% of the attention leaked onto a meaningless token and dragged the output towards the pad value. A padding mask (adding \(-\infty\) to pad columns) fixes this.

Key insight: Cross-attention is the Transformer version of Bahdanau attention: an \(m \times n\) weight matrix with no causal mask, but it still needs a padding mask.

P8.19 L3 · Application

Scaled dot-product self-attention for three tokens

A three-token sequence has embeddings (rows) \(X\), and a single head with \(d_k = d_v = 2\) uses

\[ X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad W^Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad W^K = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad W^V = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. \]

(a) Compute \(Q\), \(K\) and \(V\).

(b) Compute \(S = Q K^\top\) and the scaled scores \(S / \sqrt{d_k}\).

(c) Compute the weight matrix \(A = \operatorname{softmax}(S / \sqrt{d_k})\), row by row.

(d) Compute \(Z = A V\).

(e) Token 3's weights are exactly uniform. Explain why from its query.

Hint

Row \(i\) of \(S\) is query \(i\) dotted with every key. Use \(\sqrt{2} = 1.4142\), and remember that only the differences within a row matter for the softmax.

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ Q = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad K = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad V = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \]

(b)

\[ S = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \frac{S}{\sqrt{2}} = \begin{pmatrix} 2.1213 & 1.4142 & 2.1213 \\ 1.4142 & 2.8284 & 1.4142 \\ 1.4142 & 1.4142 & 1.4142 \end{pmatrix} \]

(c)

\[ A = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{0.4011} & \mathbf{0.1978} & \mathbf{0.4011} \\ \mathbf{0.1636} & \mathbf{0.6728} & \mathbf{0.1636} \\ \mathbf{0.3333} & \mathbf{0.3333} & \mathbf{0.3333} \end{pmatrix} \]

For example, row 1 has differences \((0, -0.7071, 0)\), so \(\alpha = (1, e^{-0.7071}, 1)/(2 + 0.4931)\).

(d)

\[ Z = A V = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{1.2033} & \mathbf{0.3956} \\ \mathbf{0.4907} & \mathbf{1.3457} \\ \mathbf{1.0000} & \mathbf{0.6667} \end{pmatrix} \]

(e) \(q_3 = (1, 1)\), and every key has entries summing to 2: \((1, 1)\), \((0, 2)\), \((1, 1)\). So \(q_3^\top k_j = k_{j1} + k_{j2} = 2\) for all \(j\), the scores are equal, and the softmax is uniform. Its output is the plain average of the values.

Key insight: In matrix form all queries are handled at once; each output row is a convex combination of the value rows, with weights read off one row of the softmax matrix.

P8.20 L3 · Application

Adding a causal mask

Use the scaled scores \(S / \sqrt{d_k}\) and the values \(V\) from P8.19.

(a) Write the masked score matrix for causal (left-to-right) attention.

(b) Compute the masked weight matrix and the output \(Z_{\text{masked}}\).

(c) Which rows changed compared with P8.19, and which did not? Explain why the first and last rows behave as they do.

(d) A language model is trained with this mask on "the cat sat". Why does the mask make it possible to compute the loss for all three next-token predictions in one parallel pass?

Hint

Entry \((i, j)\) is masked when \(j > i\). After masking, renormalise each row over the positions that remain.

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ \begin{pmatrix} 2.1213 & -\infty & -\infty \\ 1.4142 & 2.8284 & -\infty \\ 1.4142 & 1.4142 & 1.4142 \end{pmatrix} \]

(b) Row 2 is a softmax over \((1.4142, 2.8284)\), that is \((1, e^{1.4142})/(1 + 4.113)\):

\[ A_{\text{masked}} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{1} & 0 & 0 \\ \mathbf{0.1956} & \mathbf{0.8044} & 0 \\ \mathbf{0.3333} & \mathbf{0.3333} & \mathbf{0.3333} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad Z_{\text{masked}} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{2} & \mathbf{-1} \\ \mathbf{0.3911} & \mathbf{1.4133} \\ \mathbf{1} & \mathbf{0.6667} \end{pmatrix} \]

(c) Rows 1 and 2 changed; row 3 did not. Token 1 may only see itself, so its weight is 1 and its output is exactly \(v_1 = (2, -1)\), whatever the scores were. Token 3 is the last position, so nothing lies in its future and its row is untouched. The weight that row 2 used to put on token 3 (0.1636) is redistributed over tokens 1 and 2 in proportion to their exponentials.

(d) Output \(i\) depends only on tokens \(1, \dots, i\), so it can be used to predict token \(i + 1\) without having seen it. All three positions are computed in one matrix operation, and each prediction is exactly what the model would produce one token at a time at inference. With teacher forcing (true tokens as inputs), the three losses are summed in a single parallel pass, which an RNN decoder cannot do.

Key insight: The causal mask is a lower-triangular constraint that turns full self-attention into a model that never looks ahead, while keeping training fully parallel.

P8.21 L4 · Analysis

What do several heads buy over one?

(a) Show that \(h\) heads with \(d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}}/h\) plus \(W^O\) have the same number of parameters as one head with \(d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}}\) plus \(W^O\). Then show that the score computation \(Q_i K_i^\top\) summed over heads costs \(n^2 d_{\text{model}}\) multiplications, the same as one full-width head.

(b) If each of the 8 heads kept \(d_k = d_v = 512\) (with \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\)), how many parameters would the layer have, without biases?

(c) Token 3 needs the first feature of token 1 and the second feature of token 2. Suppose the values are \(v_1 = (1, 0)\) and \(v_2 = (0, 1)\) and other tokens contribute nothing useful. Show that a single head cannot output \((1, 1)\) for token 3, whatever its weights are.

(d) Show how two heads with \(d_v = 1\), followed by \(W^O = I_2\), can output exactly \((1, 1)\) if head 1 attends fully to token 1 using the first coordinate of the values and head 2 attends fully to token 2 using the second.

Hint

For (c), a single head outputs \(\alpha_1 v_1 + \alpha_2 v_2 + \dots\) with all \(\alpha_j \ge 0\) and \(\sum_j \alpha_j = 1\). What does that imply about the sum of the two output coordinates?

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Per head, \(W_i^Q, W_i^K, W_i^V\) are each \(d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}/h\), so all heads together have \(3h \cdot d_{\text{model}} \cdot d_{\text{model}}/h = 3 d_{\text{model}}^2\); \(W^O\) is \(d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}\). The total is \(4 d_{\text{model}}^2\), exactly as for one full-width head. Each head's \(Q_i K_i^\top\) costs \(n^2 d_{\text{model}}/h\), and \(h\) heads cost \(n^2 d_{\text{model}}\), the same as one head with \(d_k = d_{\text{model}}\).

(b) The projections become \(3 \times 8 \times 512 \times 512 = 6{,}291{,}456\), and \(W^O\) becomes \((8 \times 512) \times 512 = 2{,}097{,}152\), so there would be 8,388,608 parameters, 8 times the standard 1,048,576.

(c) A single head outputs \(z = \sum_j \alpha_j v_j\), so with only \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) useful, \(z = (\alpha_1, \alpha_2)\) with \(\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 \le 1\). The target \((1, 1)\) has coordinate sum 2, so it is unreachable: one softmax row has to split a single unit of weight between the two tokens, and getting more of token 1 means getting less of token 2.

(d) Head 1 uses \(W_1^V\) that keeps the first coordinate, so its values are \((1, 0, \dots)\) for tokens 1, 2, …; with weight 1 on token 1 it outputs 1. Head 2 keeps the second coordinate (\(0, 1, \dots\)) and puts weight 1 on token 2, so it outputs 1. The concatenation is \((1, 1)\), and \(W^O = I_2\) passes it through. Each head has its own softmax, so each can make a different, independent retrieval.

Key insight: For the same parameters and the same compute, multi-head attention replaces one attention pattern per token with \(h\) independent patterns, which is what lets one layer track syntax, coreference and adjacency at once.

9.F Self-attention Properties & Positional Encoding (8.6)

P8.22 L1 · Foundation

Properties of self-attention: true or false

True or false, with a reason.

(a) "Without a mask, every output \(z_i\) of a self-attention layer depends on every input \(x_j\)."

(b) "Without positional information, self-attention gives the token 'dog' the same output in 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog'."

(c) "Learned positional embeddings handle sequences longer than any seen in training."

(d) "In the original Transformer, positional encodings are added to the token embeddings, \(\tilde{x}_i = x_i + p_i\)."

(e) "The longest path a signal must travel between two positions is \(O(1)\) layers in self-attention and \(O(n)\) steps in an RNN."

(f) "The cost of one self-attention layer grows linearly with the sequence length \(n\)."

(g) "Like an RNN, a self-attention layer must process positions one after another."

Hint

Self-attention compares every pair of positions directly and uses only the content of the vectors, not their index.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. \(z_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} v_j\) with every \(\alpha_{ij} > 0\).

(b) True. "dog" has the same query, the same set of keys and the same set of values in both sentences (only their order differs), so its weighted sum is identical.

(c) False. A learned table has one vector per trained position and nothing for position 513 if training stopped at 512. Sinusoidal encodings are defined for every position.

(d) True. The encoding is added elementwise, so \(p_i\) must have size \(d_{\text{model}}\).

(e) True. Any query attends to any key directly in one layer; an RNN must carry information through every intermediate hidden state.

(f) False. The score matrix is \(n \times n\), so the cost is \(O(n^2 d)\): quadratic in \(n\).

(g) False. All rows of \(Q K^\top\) are computed in one matrix product, so all positions are processed in parallel.

Key insight: Self-attention buys direct, parallel, all-pairs interaction at a quadratic cost, and it is blind to order until positions are added to the input.

P8.23 L2 · Computation

Computing sinusoidal positional encodings

With \(d_{\text{model}} = 4\), the sinusoidal encoding is

\[ PE(pos, 2i) = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right), \qquad PE(pos, 2i + 1) = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right), \qquad i = 0, 1. \]

(a) Compute the angular frequencies \(\omega_0\) and \(\omega_1\), where \(\omega_i = 1 / 10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}\).

(b) Compute the encoding vectors for positions 0, 1, 2 and 3.

(c) Compute \(PE(10)\).

(d) Which pair of dimensions changes fastest with position, the low-index pair or the high-index pair? One slide states "lower dimensions = lower frequency". Is that right for this formula?

Hint

\(10000^{2/4} = 100\). Angles are in radians.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\omega_0 = 1\) and \(\omega_1 = 1/100 = 0.01\), so \(PE(pos) = \big(\sin pos,\ \cos pos,\ \sin(0.01\,pos),\ \cos(0.01\,pos)\big)\).

(b)

\(pos\) dim 0 dim 1 dim 2 dim 3
0 0 1 0 1
1 0.8415 0.5403 0.0100 1.0000
2 0.9093 \(-0.4161\) 0.0200 0.9998
3 0.1411 \(-0.9900\) 0.0300 0.9996

(c) \(PE(10) = (-0.5440,\ -0.8391,\ 0.0998,\ 0.9950)\).

(d) The low-index pair (dims 0 and 1) changes fastest, with wavelength \(2\pi \approx 6.3\) positions; dims 2 and 3 have wavelength \(200\pi \approx 628\) positions. So in this formula lower dimension indices have higher frequency, and the slide's wording is reversed: the low dimensions resolve fine, nearby positions and the high dimensions vary slowly and encode coarse, long-range position.

Key insight: Each pair of dimensions is a clock running at its own speed; together the fast and slow clocks give every position a distinct, bounded code.

P8.24 L3 · Application

Shuffle the tokens, shuffle the outputs

Use \(X\), \(W^Q\), \(W^K\), \(W^V\) and the result \(Z\) from P8.19, where the rows of \(X\) are tokens \(a = (1, 0, 1)\), \(b = (0, 2, 0)\), \(c = (1, 1, 0)\).

(a) Reverse the order to \((c, b, a)\), that is, \(X' = P X\) with \(P\) the permutation matrix that swaps rows 1 and 3. Without recomputing anything, predict \(Z'\). Then check its third row (token \(a\)) directly.

(b) A sentiment classifier mean-pools the outputs. Compute the pooled vector for both orders.

(c) Now add the position vectors \(p_1 = (0, 0, 0)\), \(p_2 = (0, 0, 1)\), \(p_3 = (0, 1, 0)\) to whichever token sits at each position. Compute the output of token \(a\) when it is at position 1 (original order) and when it is at position 3 (reversed order).

(d) What do (a) to (c) show?

Hint

Permuting the rows of \(X\) permutes the rows of \(Q\), \(K\) and \(V\) in the same way. For (c), work out only the query row of token \(a\) and the full \(K\) and \(V\) of each sequence.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The outputs are permuted the same way:

\[ Z' = P Z = \begin{pmatrix} 1.0000 & 0.6667 \\ 0.4907 & 1.3457 \\ 1.2033 & 0.3956 \end{pmatrix} \]

Check: token \(a\) still has \(q = (2, 1)\), and the keys are the same three vectors \((1,1), (0,2), (1,1)\) in a new order, so its scaled scores are \((2.1213, 1.4142, 2.1213)\) as a set, its weights are \((0.4011, 0.1978, 0.4011)\) on \((c, b, a)\), whose values are \((1,1), (0,2), (2,-1)\). The output is \((1.2033,\ 0.3956)\), the same as before.

(b) Both orders give \((0.8980,\ 0.8026)\). The classifier cannot tell the two orders apart.

(c) Original order with positions: \(a + p_1 = (1, 0, 1)\) has \(q = (2, 1)\); the keys are \((1, 1), (0, 3), (1, 2)\) and the values \((2, -1), (1, 1), (1, 2)\). The scaled scores \((3, 3, 4)/\sqrt{2}\) give weights \((0.2483, 0.2483, 0.5035)\) and output \((1.248,\ 1.007)\).

Reversed order with positions: \(a + p_3 = (1, 1, 1)\) has \(q = (2, 2)\); the keys are \((1, 1), (0, 3), (1, 2)\) and the values \((1, 1), (1, 1), (2, 0)\). The scaled scores \((4, 6, 6)/\sqrt{2}\) give weights \((0.1084, 0.4458, 0.4458)\) and output \((1.446,\ 0.554)\).

(d) Without positions, self-attention is permutation-equivariant: reorder the input and the output rows are reordered the same way, and any pooled summary is unchanged. Once positions are added, the same token produces different outputs at different places, so order now matters.

Key insight: Self-attention treats its input as a set; positional encodings are what turn that set back into a sequence.

P8.25 L3 · Application

Relative position from sinusoidal encodings

Use the \(d_{\text{model}} = 4\) encoding of P8.23, with \(\omega_0 = 1\) and \(\omega_1 = 0.01\).

(a) For one frequency \(\omega\), find the \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(M_k\) with

\[ \begin{pmatrix} \sin((pos + k)\omega) \\ \cos((pos + k)\omega) \end{pmatrix} = M_k \begin{pmatrix} \sin(pos\,\omega) \\ \cos(pos\,\omega) \end{pmatrix}, \]

and check that \(M_k\) does not depend on \(pos\).

(b) Evaluate \(M_2\) for \(\omega_0 = 1\) and use it to get dims 0 and 1 of \(PE(3)\) from \(PE(1)\). Compare with the table in P8.23.

(c) Show that \(PE(pos) \cdot PE(pos + k) = \sum_i \cos(k\,\omega_i)\), and evaluate it for \(k = 1, 2, 3\). Check \(k = 1\) with \(pos = 0\) and \(pos = 1\).

(d) For \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\), what are the shortest and longest wavelengths (in positions) among the 256 frequency pairs?

Hint

Use \(\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta\) and \(\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta\) with \(\alpha = pos\,\omega\), \(\beta = k\omega\). The wavelength of pair \(i\) is \(2\pi / \omega_i\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Expanding with the identities:

\[ M_k = \begin{pmatrix} \cos k\omega & \sin k\omega \\ -\sin k\omega & \cos k\omega \end{pmatrix} \]

It is a rotation by \(k\omega\), and it involves only the offset \(k\), not \(pos\).

(b) For \(\omega = 1\), \(k = 2\):

\[ M_2 = \begin{pmatrix} -0.4161 & 0.9093 \\ -0.9093 & -0.4161 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad M_2 \begin{pmatrix} 0.8415 \\ 0.5403 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{0.1411} \\ \mathbf{-0.9900} \end{pmatrix} \]

This matches dims 0 and 1 of \(PE(3)\) in P8.23.

(c) For each pair,

\[ \sin(pos\,\omega)\sin((pos + k)\omega) + \cos(pos\,\omega)\cos((pos + k)\omega) = \cos(k\omega), \]

so the dot product is \(\cos k + \cos 0.01k\). This gives 1.5403 for \(k = 1\), 0.5837 for \(k = 2\) and 0.0096 for \(k = 3\). Directly from the table, \(PE(0) \cdot PE(1) = 0.5403 + 1.0000 = 1.5403\) and \(PE(1) \cdot PE(2) = 0.7652 - 0.2248 + 0.0002 + 0.9998 \approx 1.540\). The two agree.

(d) Shortest: pair \(i = 0\), \(\omega = 1\), wavelength \(2\pi \approx 6.28\) positions. Longest: pair \(i = 255\), \(\omega = 10000^{-510/512}\), wavelength \(2\pi \times 10000^{510/512} \approx 58{,}470\) positions.

Key insight: A shift by \(k\) positions is the same linear map (a set of rotations) at every position, so a layer can learn "look \(k\) tokens back" once and apply it everywhere; and the similarity of two encodings depends only on their distance.

P8.26 L4 · Analysis

Proving permutation equivariance, and what breaks it

Let \(f(X) = \operatorname{softmax}\big(X W^Q (X W^K)^\top / \sqrt{d_k}\big)\, X W^V\) with a row-wise softmax, and let \(P\) be an \(n \times n\) permutation matrix.

(a) Show that a row-wise softmax satisfies \(\operatorname{softmax}(P S P^\top) = P\, \operatorname{softmax}(S)\, P^\top\) for any \(n \times n\) score matrix \(S\).

(b) Prove that \(f(PX) = P f(X)\).

(c) The slides write "Attention(X) = Attention(PX)" and call self-attention permutation-invariant. Is that statement exactly right? Which quantity is invariant?

(d) Explain why each of the following breaks the property: (i) a causal mask; (ii) adding positional encodings \(X + P_{\text{pos}}\) before the layer.

Hint

\(P S P^\top\) reorders the rows and the columns of \(S\) in the same way, and a permutation matrix satisfies \(P^\top P = I\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Row \(i\) of \(P S P^\top\) is row \(\pi(i)\) of \(S\) with its entries reordered by the same permutation. The softmax of a row depends only on the multiset of its entries and moves each entry's weight along with it. Applying it row by row therefore gives row \(\pi(i)\) of \(\operatorname{softmax}(S)\), with columns reordered in the same way, which is \(P\,\operatorname{softmax}(S)\,P^\top\).

(b) With \(S = X W^Q (X W^K)^\top / \sqrt{d_k}\):

\[ \begin{aligned} f(PX) &= \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{P X W^Q (P X W^K)^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) P X W^V = \operatorname{softmax}(P S P^\top)\, P X W^V \\ &= P\, \operatorname{softmax}(S)\, P^\top P\, X W^V = P\, \operatorname{softmax}(S)\, X W^V = \mathbf{P\, f(X)} \end{aligned} \]

(c) Not exactly. \(f(PX) = P f(X)\) is equivariance: the outputs are the same vectors in permuted order, as P8.24 showed. The slide's equation \(f(PX) = f(X)\) holds only for order-free summaries of the output, such as the mean or sum over tokens, \(\mathbf{1}^\top f(PX) = \mathbf{1}^\top P f(X) = \mathbf{1}^\top f(X)\). The slide's practical conclusion still stands: nothing in the layer knows which token came first.

(d) (i) The causal mask is a fixed lower-triangular pattern tied to positions; after permuting, the mask is not permuted with the tokens, so \(\operatorname{softmax}(PSP^\top + M) \ne P\,\operatorname{softmax}(S + M)\,P^\top\) in general. With the matrices of P8.19, the masked output of the reversed sequence has last row \((1.2033, 0.3956)\), whereas \(P Z_{\text{masked}}\) has last row \((2, -1)\). (ii) \(PX + P_{\text{pos}} \ne P(X + P_{\text{pos}})\), because the position vectors stay where they are while the tokens move. The input itself is no longer a permuted copy, so the argument in (b) does not apply.

Key insight: The algebra \(P^\top P = I\) is the entire reason self-attention is order-blind; anything that refers to absolute positions (masks or encodings) breaks the symmetry, and that is exactly how order is reintroduced.

P8.27 L4 · Analysis

Path length and cost: self-attention vs RNN vs CNN

Compare one layer of each architecture on a sequence of length \(n\) with width \(d = 512\).

(a) Two tokens are 1023 positions apart (\(n = 1024\)). How many sequential steps or layers must a signal pass through between them in (i) an RNN, (ii) a stack of contiguous convolutions with kernel 3, (iii) a stack of dilated convolutions with kernel 2 and dilations \(1, 2, 4, \dots\), (iv) one self-attention layer? Give the big-O form of each.

(b) Using the slides' per-layer costs \(O(n^2 d)\) for self-attention and \(O(n d^2)\) for an RNN, compute both for \(n = 128\), \(n = 512\) and \(n = 4096\). For which \(n\) does each dominate?

(c) Storing one \(n \times n\) attention matrix per head in 32-bit floats, how much memory do 8 heads need for \(n = 4096\) in a single layer?

(d) Why does a short path matter for learning, and what does the RNN offer in return?

Hint

A contiguous kernel-3 convolution grows the receptive field by 2 per layer; a kernel-2 dilated stack doubles it per layer. The two costs differ by the factor \(n/d\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) (i) 1023 steps, \(O(n)\). (ii) The receptive field after \(L\) layers is \(1 + 2L\), so \(L = 512\) layers, \(O(n/k)\). (iii) The receptive field is \(2^L\), so \(L = \log_2 1024 = 10\) layers, \(O(\log n)\). (iv) 1 layer, \(O(1)\).

(b)

\(n\) self-attention \(n^2 d\) RNN \(n d^2\) ratio \(n/d\)
128 8.39 M 33.6 M 0.25
512 134 M 134 M 1
4096 8.59 G 1.07 G 8

Self-attention is cheaper when \(n < d\), and the RNN when \(n > d\); they break even at \(n = d = 512\). Most sentences have \(n < d\), which is one reason Transformers were cheap for translation. Long documents, audio or high-resolution images have \(n \gg d\), and there attention's quadratic term dominates.

(c) \(4096^2 \times 8 \times 4\) bytes \(= 536{,}870{,}912\) bytes \(=\) 512 MiB for one layer's attention weights.

(d) Gradients between two positions must pass through every intermediate step; in an RNN that is a product of \(O(n)\) Jacobians, which vanishes or explodes (Module 7). With an \(O(1)\) path the gradient from a distant token arrives directly. In exchange, an RNN has \(O(n)\) total cost and constant memory per step, while self-attention pays \(O(n^2)\) in time and memory and gives up the built-in notion of order, which is why it needs positional encodings.

Key insight: The Transformer trades the information bottleneck of recurrence for a compute bottleneck; whether that trade is good depends on whether \(n\) is smaller or larger than \(d\).

9.G Module 8 Capstone

P8.28 L5 · Mastery

Pick the attention for the job

For each system, say which attention blocks it needs (unmasked self-attention, masked self-attention, cross-attention), where the queries, keys and values come from, and what would go wrong with the most tempting wrong choice.

(a) The encoder of a Hindi-to-English translator.

(b) The decoder of the same translator.

(c) A GPT-style language model that writes text left to right.

(d) A BERT-style sentiment classifier for product reviews.

(e) An image-captioning model whose image encoder outputs 49 feature vectors.

(f) A forecaster that, at every hour \(t\), predicts the gold price at hour \(t + 1\) from hours \(1, \dots, t\), trained on whole series at once.

Hint

Ask two questions for each: is the whole input available at once, and is there a second sequence to look at?

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Unmasked self-attention over the source tokens (Q, K, V all from the Hindi sentence), plus a padding mask. A causal mask here would be the tempting mistake: the source is fully known, so masking only throws away right-hand context, for example the verb at the end of a Hindi sentence, with no leakage to prevent.

(b) Masked self-attention over the English tokens generated so far, then cross-attention with queries from the decoder and keys/values from the encoder output. Without the mask, training with teacher forcing would let position \(t\) copy the true word \(y_{t+1}\), giving a near-zero training loss and a model that fails at inference. Without cross-attention the decoder would never see the source.

(c) Masked self-attention only; there is no second sequence, so no cross-attention. Dropping the mask is the classic bug: training loss collapses because the model reads the answer.

(d) Unmasked (bidirectional) self-attention with a padding mask, and a pooled or \(\langle\text{CLS}\rangle\) output for the classifier. A causal mask would stop early words from seeing later ones ("not bad" read as "not" then "bad" separately), hurting a task where the whole review is available.

(e) Masked self-attention over the caption so far plus cross-attention from caption tokens (queries) to the 49 image vectors (keys/values). It has the same structure as translation, with an image in place of the source sentence.

(f) Masked (causal) self-attention over the time steps. Training on whole series in parallel without the mask leaks the future price into the prediction: excellent validation numbers and a useless live model.

Key insight: Unmasked self-attention is for inputs you fully have, masked self-attention for outputs you are generating, and cross-attention whenever a second sequence must be consulted.

P8.29 L5 · Mastery

Diagnosing attention that collapses onto one token

A colleague's one-layer self-attention classifier (\(d_k = 256\)) plateaus early. Logging shows that almost every query puts more than 0.999 of its weight on a single key. For one query over a 4-token input the logged raw scores are

\[ q^\top k = (41.0,\ 18.5,\ 22.3,\ 15.1), \]

and the code computes \(\operatorname{softmax}(Q K^\top) V\).

(a) Compute the weights as the code does, their entropy \(H = -\sum_j \alpha_j \ln \alpha_j\), and \(\partial \alpha_1 / \partial e_1\).

(b) Compute the same three quantities with the scores divided by \(\sqrt{d_k}\). Compare with the maximum possible entropy for 4 tokens.

(c) After the scaling fix, in a different batch the attention still collapses, now onto position 7 of a 9-token input, and position 7 is a \(\langle\text{PAD}\rangle\) token. Predictions change when the same sentence is padded to a different length. What is the bug?

(d) List four further checks you would make if collapse persists, each with the fix it suggests.

Hint

The score gap of 18.7 between the top two keys is the whole story in (a). For (c), ask what the softmax does with a position that should not exist.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The gaps below the top score are 18.7 or more, so

\[ \alpha \approx (1 - 7.7 \times 10^{-9},\ 1.7 \times 10^{-10},\ 7.6 \times 10^{-9},\ 5.6 \times 10^{-12}), \qquad H \approx \mathbf{1.5 \times 10^{-7}}, \qquad \frac{\partial \alpha_1}{\partial e_1} \approx \mathbf{7.7 \times 10^{-9}} \]

The layer is a hard argmax, and almost no gradient reaches \(W^Q\) or \(W^K\), which explains the plateau.

(b) With scores divided by 16, \((2.5625, 1.1563, 1.3938, 0.9438)\):

\[ \alpha = (\mathbf{0.570},\ \mathbf{0.140},\ \mathbf{0.177},\ \mathbf{0.113}), \qquad H = \mathbf{1.148}, \qquad \frac{\partial \alpha_1}{\partial e_1} = \mathbf{0.245} \]

The maximum entropy is \(\ln 4 = 1.386\), so the scaled weights are still focused on key 1 but far from one-hot, and the gradient is about \(3 \times 10^7\) times larger. The missing \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) was the first bug.

(c) There is no padding mask. Pad positions get real scores, and a pad key can win the softmax (P8.18 showed even a zero key takes weight). Add \(-\infty\) to the score columns of pad positions so they get weight exactly 0; then padding length cannot change the prediction.

(d) Any four of:

  • Query and key norms. Large norms (no LayerNorm, large initialisation, embeddings scaled up) inflate scores just as a missing \(\sqrt{d_k}\) does. Fix with LayerNorm before attention, a smaller initialisation, or weight decay.
  • Collapse onto the diagonal. If every token attends to itself, \(W^Q\) and \(W^K\) may have become similar, so \(q_i^\top k_i \propto \lVert x_i \rVert^2\) dominates. Positional encodings and multiple heads help, and some models mask the diagonal.
  • Learning rate and warmup. Too large a step early in training can blow the logits up. Lower the learning rate or add warmup.
  • Is it a special token? Heavy attention on \(\langle\text{BOS}\rangle\) or \(\langle\text{CLS}\rangle\) in a trained deep model can be a benign "no-op" pattern. Check whether accuracy actually suffers before treating it as a bug.
  • Attention dropout. Dropout on the weights discourages relying on a single key.

Key insight: Attention collapse is usually a numerics or masking bug (unscaled or inflated scores, missing padding mask) rather than the model "deciding" one token matters; measure entropy and the softmax gradient before interpreting the pattern.

P8.30 L5 · Mastery

Three misconceptions about attention

Each statement below is a common misconception. For each one, explain precisely what is wrong and state the correct version.

(a) "Attention replaced RNNs because it's smarter."

(b) "The Transformer ignores word order."

(c) "Attention weights are explanations: the token with the largest weight is the reason for the prediction."

For (c), use these two facts. First, with values \(v_1 = (1, 0)\), \(v_2 = (0, 1)\), \(v_3 = (0.5, 0.5)\), compute the output for the weights \((0.5, 0.5, 0)\), \((0, 0, 1)\) and \((0.25, 0.25, 0.5)\). Second, with weights \((0.6, 0.3, 0.1)\) on values of norm \((0.5, 1, 10)\), compute each token's contribution \(\alpha_j \lVert v_j \rVert\) and its share of the total.

Hint

For (a), name the specific failure mode attention fixes. For (b), recall P8.24 and P8.26. For (c), ask whether a prediction determines the weights that produced it.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Attention was introduced to fix a specific, nameable failure: the fixed-size context vector of seq2seq RNNs (P8.2), which loses early tokens on long inputs. Self-attention then replaced recurrence for two further concrete reasons: an \(O(1)\) path between any two positions, so no vanishing gradient over distance (P8.27), and parallel computation over positions instead of \(O(n)\) sequential steps. It is not "smarter" in any general sense, and it pays for these gains with \(O(n^2)\) cost and no built-in order.

(b) Bare self-attention is order-blind (permutation-equivariant, P8.26), but the Transformer adds positional encodings precisely to inject order, and a decoder's causal mask also depends on position. With positions added, the same word produces different outputs at different places (P8.24). The correct statement: self-attention alone ignores order; the Transformer puts order back in explicitly, and removing or corrupting the positional encoding breaks order-sensitive tasks.

(c) All three weight vectors give the same output, \((0.5, 0.5)\), so very different "explanations" produce an identical prediction; the weights are not identifiable from the behaviour. In the second case the contributions are \((0.3, 0.3, 1.0)\) with shares \((0.1875, 0.1875, 0.625)\): the token with the smallest weight, 0.1, contributes most because its value is large. Beyond these, after the first layer each value is already a mixture of many tokens, and there are many heads and layers plus a feed-forward network after attention. Correct version: attention weights show where one head read from at one layer; they are a useful diagnostic, but a claim about why the model predicted something needs evidence such as ablating tokens or gradient-based attribution.

Key insight: Good explanations of attention are specific: it fixes a named bottleneck, it needs positions added to see order, and its weights describe information routing, not causation.

P8.31 L5 · Mastery

A two-head causal layer with positions, end to end

A toy language model reads the tokens "A B C" with embeddings \(A = (1, 0, 0, 1)\), \(B = (0, 1, 1, 0)\), \(C = (1, 1, 0, 0)\) and adds the \(d_{\text{model}} = 4\) sinusoidal encodings of P8.23 for positions 0, 1, 2. One masked multi-head layer has two heads with \(d_k = d_v = 2\): head 1 uses coordinates 1–2 of each row as its query, key and value, and head 2 uses coordinates 3–4 (that is, \(W_1^Q = W_1^K = W_1^V\) selects the first two coordinates and similarly for head 2). The output projection is \(W^O = I_4\).

(a) Form the input matrix \(X = E + PE\).

(b) Compute both heads' attention weights for token 3 and its layer output \(z_3\).

(c) What is \(z_1\), and why can you write it down without computing any softmax?

(d) Without positional encodings, compute \(z_3\) for "A B C" and for "B A C". Then, with positional encodings, compute \(z_3\) for "B A C" and compare with (b). What does this say about a causal model's ability to use order?

(e) This layer ties \(W^Q = W^K\) in each head and uses \(W^O = I\). Name one kind of relationship each of these choices prevents the layer from learning.

Hint

Token 3 is the last position, so the causal mask removes nothing from its row. For (d), what set of tokens does position 3 see in each order?

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0.8415 & 1.5403 & 1.0100 & 1.0000 \\ 1.9093 & 0.5839 & 0.0200 & 0.9998 \end{pmatrix} \]

(b) Head 1 (coordinates 1–2): token 3's scaled scores are \((1.7629,\ 1.7720,\ 2.8187)\), so its weights are \(\mathbf{(0.2048,\ 0.2066,\ 0.5886)}\) and its output is \((1.5024,\ 0.8667)\). Head 2 (coordinates 3–4): the scores \((1.4139,\ 0.7212,\ 0.7071)\) give weights \(\mathbf{(0.5016,\ 0.2509,\ 0.2474)}\) and output \((0.2584,\ 1.5016)\). Concatenating and applying \(W^O = I\):

\[ z_3 = (\mathbf{1.5024},\ \mathbf{0.8667},\ \mathbf{0.2584},\ \mathbf{1.5016}) \]

The two heads look at different places: head 1 mostly at token 3 itself, head 2 mostly at token 1.

(c) \(z_1 = x_1 = (1, 1, 0, 2)\). Under the causal mask, token 1 can only attend to itself, so each head's weight on it is 1 and returns its own value slice.

(d) Without positions, \(z_3 = \mathbf{(0.7517,\ 0.7517,\ 0.3333,\ 0.3333)}\) for both orders: position 3 sees the same set \(\{A, B, C\}\) in both orders, and attention over a set ignores its order. With positions, "B A C" gives \(z_3 = \mathbf{(1.7514,\ 0.6596,\ 0.2609,\ 1.5016)}\), which differs from (b). The causal mask does carry some order information, since tokens 1 and 2 see different prefixes, but the last token's view of its prefix is order-blind. A causal model still needs positional encodings to tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog" when predicting the next word.

(e) With \(W^Q = W^K\) the raw score matrix is symmetric, \(q_i^\top k_j = q_j^\top k_i\), so the layer cannot learn asymmetric relations, such as "a pronoun attends strongly to its antecedent, but the antecedent does not attend to the pronoun". With \(W^O = I\) the heads' outputs are merely stacked, so the layer cannot combine features found by different heads (for example, syntax from one head and position from another) into the same output coordinates. Learned, distinct \(W^Q\), \(W^K\), \(W^V\) and \(W^O\) remove both limits.

Key insight: A real attention layer is the sum of everything in this module: scaled scores, a mask, several heads with their own softmaxes, positional encodings to break the set symmetry, and learned projections that make relations asymmetric and let heads be mixed.

P8.32 L5 · Mastery

Choosing an architecture for long-document summarisation

You must summarise 2000-token reports into 100-token summaries, with model width \(d = 512\). Three designs are on the table:

  • (A) an LSTM encoder–decoder with no attention (context vector of size 512);
  • (B) a bidirectional LSTM encoder with Bahdanau attention in the decoder;
  • (C) a Transformer encoder–decoder with 6 encoder layers of 8-head self-attention.

(a) For (A), how many context numbers does the decoder get per input token? What will the summaries miss?

(b) For (B), how many alignment scores are computed per summary? What does the decoder now have access to, and what bottleneck remains in the encoder?

(c) For (C), how many entries does one head's encoder self-attention matrix have? How much memory, in 32-bit floats, do the matrices of all heads in all 6 encoder layers need for one document? Compare the per-layer costs \(n^2 d\) and \(n d^2\).

(d) Write a short recommendation: which design you would choose, under what memory budget, and one modification that would make (C) cheaper. Frame it in terms of which bottleneck each design removes and which new one it creates.

Hint

Bahdanau attention computes \(T \times T'\) scores. For (C) use \(n = 2000\) and remember that the attention matrix is \(n \times n\) per head per layer.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(512 / 2000 =\) 0.256 numbers per input token. As in P8.2, the early part of the report is mostly overwritten by the end, so the summaries will over-represent the last few sentences and miss key facts from the start.

(b) \(T \times T' = 2000 \times 100 =\) 200,000 scores per summary. The decoder now reads all 2000 encoder states directly, so the context-vector bottleneck is gone. The encoder is still an RNN: it must process 2000 steps sequentially (slow, not parallel over positions), and relations between distant parts of the report must pass through \(O(n)\) recurrent steps, so long-range structure within the document is still weakly modelled.

(c) \(2000^2 =\) 4,000,000 entries per head per layer. All matrices together take

\[ 4 \times 10^6 \times 8 \times 6 \times 4 \text{ bytes} = 768{,}000{,}000 \text{ bytes} \approx \mathbf{732\ MiB} \]

per document, before activations for backprop and before the decoder. Per layer, \(n^2 d = 2.05 \times 10^9\) against \(n d^2 = 5.24 \times 10^8\): with \(n > d\), self-attention costs about 3.9 times more arithmetic than a recurrent layer, but all of it is parallel.

(d) A reasonable recommendation: (A) is ruled out by the context bottleneck. With ample GPU memory (several GB per document after batching), (C) gives the best long-range modelling, with an \(O(1)\) path between any two tokens, and parallel training. With a tight budget, (B) is a defensible choice: it removes the decoder's bottleneck at a cost linear in \(n\) per decoder step. To make (C) cheaper, use local (windowed) or sparse attention, or encode the report in chunks of, say, 512 tokens, which cuts the \(n^2\) term by roughly the number of chunks. In terms of bottlenecks: (A) has an information bottleneck; (B) removes it for the decoder but keeps a sequential encoder; (C) removes recurrence altogether and pays with an \(O(n^2)\) compute and memory cost.

Key insight: Each step from seq2seq to attention to the Transformer removes one bottleneck and introduces another; the right design depends on whether information loss, sequential time or quadratic memory is the binding constraint for your sequence length.

PART 10 — Module 9: Transformer

Conventions used throughout this module (they match the Module 9 deck). Tokens are row vectors. We write \(d = d_{\text{model}}\) for the embedding width, \(h\) for the number of heads, \(d_k = d_v = d/h\) for the per-head width, and \(d_{ff} = 4d\) for the FFN hidden width. \(n\) is the source (encoder) length, \(m\) the target (decoder) length, \(B\) the batch size, \(N\) the number of stacked layers and \(V\) the vocabulary size (the deck writes \(\lvert V \rvert\)). The deck uses the pre-LN layout:

\[ Z_1 = X + \operatorname{MHA}(\operatorname{LN}(X)), \qquad Z_2 = Z_1 + \operatorname{FFN}(\operatorname{LN}(Z_1)), \]

and a decoder layer inserts \(Z_2 = Z_1 + \operatorname{CrossAttn}(\operatorname{LN}(Z_1), H_{\text{enc}})\) between masked self-attention and the FFN. \(\operatorname{LN}(x) = \gamma \odot \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta\), with \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) taken over the \(d\) features of one token (population variance, divide by \(d\)); \(\epsilon\) is ignored in hand calculations unless stated. The FFN is \(\operatorname{FFN}(x) = \operatorname{ReLU}(x W_1 + b_1) W_2 + b_2\) (ViT uses GELU instead).

Parameter-counting convention. An "exact" count includes a bias on every linear map and \(\gamma, \beta\) on every LayerNorm. The deck's estimates (slides "Transformer Encoder: Parameters" and "Transformer Decoder: Parameters") count only the weight matrices plus the LayerNorm vectors, which gives the leading terms \(\approx 12 d^2\) per encoder layer and \(\approx 16 d^2\) per decoder layer. With biases the exact values are

\[ \text{encoder layer} = 12 d^2 + 13 d, \qquad \text{decoder layer (with cross-attention)} = 16 d^2 + 19 d. \]

Memory is in bytes, with 4 bytes per fp32 number and 2 per fp16 number; 1 MB = \(10^6\) bytes and 1 GB = \(10^9\) bytes. Logarithms are natural. One small erratum: the slide "Transformer Encoder: Encoder Input" says the embedding and positional encoding are concatenated, but its own equation \(X = \operatorname{Embedding}(\text{tokens}) + \operatorname{PE}(\text{positions})\) adds them. Addition is correct, and it is why both must have width \(d\).

10.A Why Transformers & the Block Diagram (9.1–9.2)

P9.1 L1 · Foundation

What the Transformer fixes, and what it does not

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "An RNN layer needs \(n\) sequential steps to process a length-\(n\) sequence, however many GPU cores are available."

(b) "LSTMs and GRUs fully solve long-range dependencies, so the Transformer was motivated only by training speed."

(c) "In one self-attention layer, information from token 1 reaches token \(n\) after passing through \(n - 1\) intermediate hidden states."

(d) "Because the Transformer has no recurrence, it has no way of knowing word order."

(e) "Attending to all tokens removes the RNN's fixed-size memory bottleneck at no extra cost."

(f) "Being parallel across positions is what made it practical to train Transformers on very large corpora."

Hint

The deck names three RNN problems: sequential processing, vanishing gradients over long ranges, and a fixed-size hidden state. For each statement, ask which of the three it is about and what the Transformer pays for its fix.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. \(h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)\) cannot start before \(h_{t-1}\) exists, so the time loop is inherently serial.

(b) False. Gated RNNs help, but the deck notes that they still struggle beyond roughly 100–200 tokens, and they keep the other two problems (serial compute, a fixed-size state).

(c) False. Every token attends to every other token directly, so the path length is 1 per layer, not \(n - 1\).

(d) False. Self-attention by itself is permutation-equivariant, which is exactly why a positional encoding is added to the input embeddings. With the encoding, order is known.

(e) False. The bottleneck is gone (the decoder can see all \(n\) encoder states), but the attention matrix has \(n \times n\) entries per head, so memory and compute grow as \(O(n^2)\).

(f) True. All positions of a layer are computed in one batched matrix multiply, which is what let models scale to trillions of training tokens.

Key insight: The Transformer swaps the RNN's information bottleneck and serial loop for a quadratic attention cost; it solves three problems and introduces one.

P9.2 L1 · Foundation

Reading the encoder and decoder block diagram

Using the deck's block diagram for "the cat sat on the mat" (encoder) and its target sequence (decoder):

(a) List the sub-layers of one encoder layer and of one decoder layer, in order.

(b) How many residual additions and how many LayerNorms does one encoder layer contain? One decoder layer?

(c) Which decoder sub-layer receives \(H_{\text{enc}}\), and does \(H_{\text{enc}}\) supply the queries or the keys and values?

(d) During training on the target "the cat sat on the mat", what token sequence is fed into the decoder and what sequence is it trained to predict?

(e) Give the shapes of the encoder output, the decoder output and the final output-layer result for a source of length \(n\) and a target of length \(m\).

Hint

Each sub-layer is wrapped as "LayerNorm, sub-layer, add the input back". The decoder input is the target shifted right by one position.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Encoder layer: multi-head self-attention, then the position-wise FFN. Decoder layer: masked multi-head self-attention, then cross-attention to \(H_{\text{enc}}\), then the FFN.

(b) Encoder: 2 residual additions and 2 LayerNorms. Decoder: 3 and 3, one per sub-layer.

(c) The cross-attention sub-layer. The queries come from the decoder stream, \(Q = \operatorname{LN}(Z_1) W^Q\); \(H_{\text{enc}}\) supplies the keys and values, \(K = H_{\text{enc}} W^K\), \(V = H_{\text{enc}} W^V\).

(d) The decoder input is "<s> the cat sat on the" and the targets are "the cat sat on the mat": position \(t\) predicts token \(t + 1\) of the input stream.

(e) \(H_{\text{enc}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\), decoder output \(D^{(N)} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}\), and after the output Linear + softmax, \(m \times V\) probabilities (one distribution over the vocabulary per target position).

Key insight: The encoder has two sub-layers and the decoder three; the extra one, cross-attention, is the only place where the two stacks talk to each other.

P9.3 L3 · Application

Serial steps, path length and memory: RNN versus Transformer

A document has \(n = 1000\) tokens. Compare a single-layer RNN with hidden size 1024 against a Transformer encoder layer with \(d = 512\) and \(h = 8\) heads.

(a) How many sequential steps does each need to process the whole document in one layer?

(b) What is the length of the computational path from token 1 to the representation of token 1000 in each?

(c) As a toy model, suppose each RNN transition multiplies the backpropagated gradient by 0.9. By what factor is the gradient from the loss at token 1000 scaled by the time it reaches token 1? What replaces this product in self-attention?

(d) How many numbers does each model hand to a decoder as its summary of the document (the RNN's final hidden state versus the whole encoder output)? What is the ratio?

(e) What is the price? Compute the number of attention-matrix entries in this one encoder layer (all heads, one document), and the fp32 memory they take.

Hint

For (c), the RNN gradient is a product of 999 factors. For (e), each head builds its own \(n \times n\) matrix.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) RNN: 1000 sequential steps. Transformer layer: 1 step, since all 1000 positions are computed together as one matrix product.

(b) RNN: 999 transitions. Self-attention: 1, since token 1000's query looks directly at token 1's key.

(c) The RNN factor is

\[ 0.9^{999} \approx \mathbf{1.9 \times 10^{-46}}, \]

which is zero in any floating-point sense. In self-attention, the gradient reaches token 1 through a single attention weight and the value projection, with no product over 999 steps.

(d) RNN: 1024 numbers, whatever the length. Encoder: \(n \times d = 1000 \times 512 =\) 512,000 numbers, a ratio of 500, and it keeps growing with \(n\).

(e) Each head holds \(1000 \times 1000 = 10^6\) entries, so the layer holds

\[ 8 \times 10^6 \text{ entries} \times 4 \text{ bytes} = \mathbf{32 \text{ MB}} \]

per document, per layer. Doubling the length to 2000 tokens would multiply this by 4.

Key insight: Path length 1 fixes the vanishing gradient over distance, and an \(n \times d\) memory fixes the fixed-size bottleneck; both come from the same \(n \times n\) attention matrix, which is also the Transformer's main cost.

10.B Encoder Internals (9.3)

P9.4 L1 · Foundation

Encoder components: true or false

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "The input embedding is a learned matrix \(E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}\); looking up a token means selecting one of its rows."

(b) "The positional encoding is concatenated to the token embedding, so the encoder input is \(2d\) wide."

(c) "With \(d = 768\) and \(h = 12\) heads, multi-head attention has 12 times as many parameters as single-head attention of the same \(d\)."

(d) "'Position-wise' FFN means each position has its own FFN weights."

(e) "LayerNorm in the encoder normalises each feature across the examples in the batch."

(f) "LayerNorm performs exactly the same computation at training and at test time."

(g) "Remove the FFNs and the stack still has a non-linearity, but only the one inside the attention softmax; the FFN supplies the per-token ReLU non-linearity and about two thirds of each layer's parameters."

Hint

For (c), write down the shapes of \(W^Q_h\) for one head and stack them across heads. For (e), recall which axis the deck's LayerNorm formula averages over.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. \(E\) has one learned \(d\)-dimensional row per vocabulary entry.

(b) False. The slide's wording says "concatenate", but its equation adds: \(X = \operatorname{Embedding}(\text{tokens}) + \operatorname{PE}(\text{positions})\). The input stays \(d\) wide.

(c) False. Each head has \(W^Q_h \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_k}\) with \(d_k = d/h\); stacking the \(h\) heads gives one \(d \times d\) matrix. Splitting into heads divides the width, so the count stays \(4d^2\) (plus biases) for any \(h\).

(d) False. The same \(W_1, b_1, W_2, b_2\) are applied to every position independently, like a \(1 \times 1\) convolution over the sequence.

(e) False. It normalises across the \(d\) features of one token; that is BatchNorm's axis that the statement describes.

(f) True. The statistics come from the token itself, so there are no running averages and no train/test switch.

(g) True. The FFN holds \(8d^2\) of the \(\approx 12d^2\) weights per layer, and its ReLU (GELU in ViT) is the per-token non-linearity.

Key insight: The encoder is built from four parts with distinct jobs: embedding + position (what and where), attention (tokens communicate), FFN (each token computes on its own), and Add & Norm (keeps the deep stack trainable).

P9.5 L2 · Computation

Sinusoidal positional encoding by hand

Use the deck's encoding with \(d = 4\):

\[ \operatorname{PE}(pos, 2i) = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right), \qquad \operatorname{PE}(pos, 2i + 1) = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right). \]

(a) What are the two angular frequencies \(1/10000^{2i/d}\) for \(i = 0\) and \(i = 1\)?

(b) Compute \(\operatorname{PE}(0)\), \(\operatorname{PE}(1)\) and \(\operatorname{PE}(2)\) to four decimals.

(c) The token at position 2 has embedding \(e = (0.2,\ -0.1,\ 0.5,\ 0.3)\). What vector enters the first encoder layer?

(d) Compute \(\operatorname{PE}(0) \cdot \operatorname{PE}(1)\), \(\operatorname{PE}(1) \cdot \operatorname{PE}(2)\) and \(\operatorname{PE}(0) \cdot \operatorname{PE}(2)\). What do you notice, and why does it happen?

Hint

With \(d = 4\), the exponent \(2i/d\) is 0 or 0.5. For (d), pair the sine and cosine at the same frequency and use \(\sin a \sin b + \cos a \cos b = \cos(a - b)\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(i = 0\): 1. \(i = 1\): \(1/10000^{0.5} =\) 0.01. So \(\operatorname{PE}(pos) = (\sin pos,\ \cos pos,\ \sin 0.01 pos,\ \cos 0.01 pos)\).

(b)

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{PE}(0) &= (0,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1), \\ \operatorname{PE}(1) &= (\mathbf{0.8415},\ \mathbf{0.5403},\ \mathbf{0.0100},\ \mathbf{0.99995}), \\ \operatorname{PE}(2) &= (\mathbf{0.9093},\ \mathbf{-0.4161},\ \mathbf{0.0200},\ \mathbf{0.9998}). \end{aligned} \]

(c) The two are added element-wise:

\[ x_2 = e + \operatorname{PE}(2) = (\mathbf{1.1093},\ \mathbf{-0.5161},\ \mathbf{0.5200},\ \mathbf{1.2998}). \]

(d) \(\operatorname{PE}(0) \cdot \operatorname{PE}(1) = \operatorname{PE}(1) \cdot \operatorname{PE}(2) =\) 1.5403, and \(\operatorname{PE}(0) \cdot \operatorname{PE}(2) =\) 0.5837. Pairing each sine with its cosine,

\[ \operatorname{PE}(p) \cdot \operatorname{PE}(q) = \cos(p - q) + \cos\big(0.01 (p - q)\big), \]

so the dot product depends only on the offset \(p - q\): \(\cos 1 + \cos 0.01 = 1.5403\) for offset 1 and \(\cos 2 + \cos 0.02 = 0.5837\) for offset 2.

Key insight: Sinusoidal encodings give every position a unique code whose similarity to another position depends only on the distance between them, which is what lets attention pick up relative order. They also add no parameters.

P9.6 L2 · Computation

LayerNorm on one token, then Add & Norm

One token's vector in a \(d = 4\) model is \(x = (4,\ 0,\ -2,\ 6)\). The first LayerNorm of the layer has \(\gamma = (1,\ 1,\ 2,\ 0.5)\) and \(\beta = (0,\ 0.5,\ 0,\ -1)\). Ignore \(\epsilon\).

(a) Compute the mean \(\mu\) and the variance \(\sigma^2\) of \(x\) over its features.

(b) Compute the normalised vector \(\hat{x} = (x - \mu)/\sigma\).

(c) Compute \(\operatorname{LN}(x) = \gamma \odot \hat{x} + \beta\).

(d) The attention sub-layer, applied to \(\operatorname{LN}(x)\), returns \(s = (0.5,\ -1,\ 1,\ 0)\) for this token. Using the deck's \(Z_1 = X + \operatorname{MHA}(\operatorname{LN}(X))\), what is \(Z_1\) for this token?

(e) The next sub-layer sees \(\operatorname{LN}(Z_1)\). Compute the normalised \(\hat{z}_1\) (before the second LayerNorm's own \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\)).

(f) How many learnable parameters do the two LayerNorms of this layer have?

Hint

Use the population variance (divide by \(d = 4\)). In (d), the residual adds the sub-layer output to the un-normalised input.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\mu = (4 + 0 - 2 + 6)/4 =\) 2 and \(\sigma^2 = (2^2 + 2^2 + 4^2 + 4^2)/4 =\) 10, so \(\sigma = 3.1623\).

(b)

\[ \hat{x} = \frac{(2,\ -2,\ -4,\ 4)}{3.1623} = (\mathbf{0.6325},\ \mathbf{-0.6325},\ \mathbf{-1.2649},\ \mathbf{1.2649}). \]

Check: \(\hat{x}\) has mean 0 and variance 1.

(c)

\[ \operatorname{LN}(x) = (0.6325,\ -0.6325 + 0.5,\ 2 \times (-1.2649),\ 0.5 \times 1.2649 - 1) = (\mathbf{0.6325},\ \mathbf{-0.1325},\ \mathbf{-2.5298},\ \mathbf{-0.3675}). \]

(d) \(Z_1 = x + s =\) \((4.5,\ -1,\ -1,\ 6)\). The normalised copy was only the sub-layer's input; the residual stream carries the raw \(x\).

(e) \(\mu = 2.125\), \(\sigma^2 = 10.046875\), \(\sigma = 3.1697\), so

\[ \hat{z}_1 = (\mathbf{0.7493},\ \mathbf{-0.9859},\ \mathbf{-0.9859},\ \mathbf{1.2225}). \]

(f) Each LayerNorm has \(\gamma, \beta \in \mathbb{R}^d\), so \(2 \times 2d =\) 16 parameters (the deck's \(4d\)).

With \(\epsilon = 10^{-5}\) the answers change only in the sixth decimal place.

Key insight: LayerNorm needs only the one token, so it works for any batch size or sequence length; in the pre-LN layout the residual stream itself is never normalised, only the copy fed to each sub-layer.

P9.7 L2 · Computation

Exact parameter count of one encoder layer

An encoder layer has \(d = 512\), \(h = 8\) heads, \(d_{ff} = 2048\), biases on every linear map, and two LayerNorms.

(a) Count the multi-head attention parameters (\(W^Q, W^K, W^V, W^O\) with their biases).

(b) Count the FFN parameters (\(W_1, b_1, W_2, b_2\)).

(c) Count the LayerNorm parameters.

(d) Give the exact total and compare it with the deck's estimate \(12 d^2\). What is the difference, in parameters and as a percentage?

(e) What do 6 such layers hold?

(f) If the layer used \(h = 16\) heads instead of 8, how would the total change?

Hint

Each projection is \(d \times d\) plus a length-\(d\) bias. The FFN is \(d \to 4d \to d\), with a bias at each width.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(4(d^2 + d) = 4(262{,}144 + 512) =\) 1,050,624.

(b)

\[ d \cdot 4d + 4d + 4d \cdot d + d = 8d^2 + 5d = 2{,}097{,}152 + 2{,}560 = \mathbf{2{,}099{,}712}. \]

(c) \(2 \times 2d =\) 2,048.

(d) Exact total:

\[ 12 d^2 + 13 d = 3{,}145{,}728 + 6{,}656 = \mathbf{3{,}152{,}384}. \]

The estimate \(12 d^2 = 3{,}145{,}728\) misses 6,656 parameters, 0.21% of the layer: the biases and LayerNorm vectors are linear in \(d\) while the weights are quadratic.

(e) \(6 \times 3{,}152{,}384 =\) 18,914,304.

(f) No change. Heads split \(d\) into \(h\) slices of \(d_k = d/h\); the projections remain \(d \times d\) in total.

Note that the FFN is 66.6% of the layer and attention 33.3%.

Key insight: Per-layer size is fixed by \(d\) alone (\(\approx 12 d^2\)), with two thirds in the FFN; the head count and the sequence length do not appear in the parameter count.

P9.8 L3 · Application

Tracing tensor shapes through an encoder layer

A batch of \(B = 8\) sequences, each padded to \(n = 128\) tokens, passes through an encoder layer with \(d = 512\), \(h = 8\) heads and \(d_{ff} = 2048\). Shapes are written batch-first.

(a) What are the shapes of the token-id tensor and of \(X\) after embedding plus positional encoding?

(b) What is the shape of \(Q = \operatorname{LN}(X) W^Q\), and what is it after splitting into heads?

(c) What is the shape of the score tensor \(Q_h K_h^\top / \sqrt{d_k}\), and what number is the scale factor?

(d) Give the shapes after multiplying by \(V_h\), after concatenating the heads, and after \(W^O\).

(e) Give the shapes of the FFN hidden activation and of the layer output.

(f) How much fp32 memory do the attention probabilities (all heads, whole batch) and the FFN hidden activations take in this layer?

(g) Repeat (f) for \(n = 1024\). For what \(n\) are the two tensors the same size (for any \(B\))?

Hint

Splitting into heads only reshapes the last axis \(512 = 8 \times 64\) and moves the head axis forward. The score tensor has one \(n \times n\) matrix per head per sequence.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Token ids: \((8, 128)\) integers. \(X\): \((8, 128, 512)\).

(b) \(Q\): \((8, 128, 512)\); split into heads, \((8, 8, 128, 64)\), which is (batch, head, position, \(d_k\)). \(K\) and \(V\) have the same shapes.

(c) Scores: \((8, 8, 128, 128)\), scaled by \(1/\sqrt{64} =\) 1/8. The softmax runs over the last axis, so each row sums to 1.

(d) After \(\times V_h\): \((8, 8, 128, 64)\). After concatenation: \((8, 128, 512)\). After \(W^O\): \((8, 128, 512)\), which can be added back to \(X\).

(e) FFN hidden: \((8, 128, 2048)\). Layer output: \((8, 128, 512)\), the same as the input, which is what makes the layers stackable.

(f) Attention probabilities: \(8 \cdot 8 \cdot 128 \cdot 128 = 1{,}048{,}576\) entries, so 4.19 MB. FFN hidden: \(8 \cdot 128 \cdot 2048 = 2{,}097{,}152\) entries, so 8.39 MB.

(g) With \(n = 1024\): attention \(8 \cdot 8 \cdot 1024^2 = 67{,}108{,}864\) entries, 268.4 MB (64 times more, because \(n\) grew 8 times), while the FFN hidden grows linearly to \(16{,}777{,}216\) entries, 67.1 MB. They are equal when

\[ B h n^2 = B n \cdot 4d \quad \Rightarrow \quad n = \frac{4d}{h} = \frac{2048}{8} = \mathbf{256}. \]

Key insight: Every tensor in the layer is linear in \(n\) except the per-head \(n \times n\) attention matrix; past \(n = 4d/h\) it is the largest activation in the layer, and it grows four times for every doubling of the context.

P9.9 L3 · Application

LayerNorm versus BatchNorm on the same tensor

Three tokens (rows) with \(d = 4\) features (columns) arrive together in one batch:

\[ X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 & 5 & 7 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 & 10 \\ 0 & 4 & 8 & 4 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Take \(\gamma = 1\), \(\beta = 0\) and ignore \(\epsilon\).

(a) Apply LayerNorm. Give each row's mean and variance and the normalised matrix.

(b) Apply BatchNorm (normalise each feature across the three tokens). Give each column's mean and variance and the normalised matrix.

(c) What does BatchNorm output for token 1, and why?

(d) Now token 3 is removed and the batch holds only tokens 1 and 2. Recompute token 1's output under both normalisations.

(e) Use (d) to give two reasons why Transformers use LayerNorm.

Hint

LayerNorm reduces along a row and BatchNorm along a column. Use the population variance in both.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Row means are 4, 4, 4 and variances 5, 12, 8:

\[ \operatorname{LN}(X) = \begin{pmatrix} -1.3416 & -0.4472 & 0.4472 & 1.3416 \\ -0.5774 & -0.5774 & -0.5774 & 1.7321 \\ -1.4142 & 0 & 1.4142 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. \]

(b) Column means are \((1, 3, 5, 7)\) and variances \((0.6667, 0.6667, 6, 6)\):

\[ \operatorname{BN}(X) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1.2247 & -1.2247 & -1.2247 & 1.2247 \\ -1.2247 & 1.2247 & 1.2247 & -1.2247 \end{pmatrix}. \]

(c) All zeros. Token 1 equals the batch mean in every feature, so BatchNorm erases it entirely; its output says only "I am average for this batch".

(d) LayerNorm: token 1 is unchanged, \((-1.3416, -0.4472, 0.4472, 1.3416)\), since only its own row is used. BatchNorm: the column means become \((1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 8.5)\) and variances \((0.25, 0.25, 2.25, 2.25)\), so token 1 becomes \((-1, 1, 1, -1)\). Same token, different output, because its neighbours changed.

(e) First, a token's representation should not depend on which other sentences share its batch, or on how much padding is in it; with LayerNorm it does not. Second, during generation the decoder processes one new token at a time (batch statistics over one example are meaningless), and LayerNorm needs no running averages, so training and inference compute the same function.

Key insight: The two layers have the same formula but reduce over different axes: BatchNorm makes each example depend on the rest of the batch, and LayerNorm makes each token depend only on itself.

P9.10 L3 · Application

Counting BERT-base from its configuration

BERT-base is an encoder-only stack with \(V = 30{,}522\) WordPiece tokens, \(d = 768\), \(N = 12\) layers, \(h = 12\) heads and \(d_{ff} = 3072\). It uses learned position embeddings for up to \(n_{\max} = 512\) positions, 2 learned segment (sentence A/B) embeddings, one LayerNorm after the summed embeddings, and a "pooler" (a \(d \times d\) linear layer with bias) on top. Every linear map has a bias.

(a) Count the embedding block (token, position, segment and the embedding LayerNorm).

(b) Count one encoder layer exactly, then all 12, and compare with \(N \cdot 12 d^2\).

(c) Add the pooler and give the total. Compare it with the published figure of about 110M.

(d) What fraction of BERT-base sits in the embedding block?

(e) BERT-large has \(d = 1024\), \(N = 24\), \(h = 16\), with everything else the same. Give its total and its embedding fraction.

Hint

Use \(12 d^2 + 13 d\) for each layer. The embedding tables are \(V \times d\), \(n_{\max} \times d\) and \(2 \times d\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ 30{,}522 \cdot 768 + 512 \cdot 768 + 2 \cdot 768 + 2 \cdot 768 = 23{,}440{,}896 + 393{,}216 + 1{,}536 + 1{,}536 = \mathbf{23{,}837{,}184}. \]

(b) One layer: \(12 \cdot 768^2 + 13 \cdot 768 =\) 7,087,872. Twelve layers: 85,054,464. The estimate \(12 \cdot 12 \cdot 768^2 = 84{,}934{,}656\) is 0.14% low.

(c) The pooler adds \(768^2 + 768 = 590{,}592\), giving

\[ 23{,}837{,}184 + 85{,}054{,}464 + 590{,}592 = \mathbf{109{,}482{,}240} \approx 110\text{M}, \]

which matches the published size.

(d) \(23{,}837{,}184 / 109{,}482{,}240 =\) 21.8%, almost all of it the token table.

(e) One layer: \(12 \cdot 1024^2 + 13 \cdot 1024 = 12{,}596{,}224\); 24 layers: 302,309,376. Embeddings: \(31{,}254{,}528 + 524{,}288 + 2{,}048 + 2{,}048 = 31{,}782{,}912\). Pooler: 1,049,600. Total 335,141,888, about 335M (the deck rounds BERT-large to 340M). Embedding fraction 9.5%.

Key insight: The layers scale as \(N d^2\) and the embeddings as \(V d\), so the vocabulary is a large share of a small model and a small share of a big one.

P9.11 L4 · Analysis

Why residual connections and LayerNorm keep a deep stack trainable

A 12-layer encoder has 24 sub-layers. In the deck's pre-LN form, each sub-layer computes \(Z = X + F(\operatorname{LN}(X))\), where \(F\) is attention or the FFN.

(a) Write the Jacobian \(\partial Z / \partial X\) of one sub-layer in terms of \(J_F\) and \(J_{\text{LN}}\).

(b) For a stack of \(K\) sub-layers with \(A_k = J_{F_k} J_{\text{LN}_k}\), write \(\partial Z_K / \partial X\) and expand the product. Which term guarantees that \(\partial L / \partial X\) cannot vanish?

(c) Take a scalar toy model in which the sub-layer slopes alternate \(a_k = +0.3, -0.3, +0.3, \dots\) over \(K = 24\) sub-layers. Compute the end-to-end gradient factor without residuals (\(\prod a_k\)) and with residuals (\(\prod (1 + a_k)\)).

(d) What does the LayerNorm in front of each \(F\) add to this argument?

(e) The residual addition puts a constraint on every sub-layer's output shape. What is it, and which two design choices in the encoder exist to satisfy it?

Hint

The derivative of \(X + G(X)\) is \(I + J_G\). For (c), group the 24 factors into 12 pairs.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) By the chain rule,

\[ \frac{\partial Z}{\partial X} = I + J_F\, J_{\text{LN}}. \]

(b)

\[ \frac{\partial Z_K}{\partial X} = \prod_{k=K}^{1} (I + A_k) = I + \sum_k A_k + \sum_{j > k} A_j A_k + \cdots \]

The leading identity term means \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial X} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial Z_K} + (\text{other terms})\): the top-layer gradient reaches the bottom unchanged, whatever the sub-layers do. These are the deck's "gradient highways".

(c) Without residuals the magnitude is \(0.3^{24} \approx\) \(2.8 \times 10^{-13}\), gone. With residuals,

\[ \prod_{k=1}^{24} (1 + a_k) = (1.3 \times 0.7)^{12} = 0.91^{12} \approx \mathbf{0.32}, \]

which is still of order 1 after 24 sub-layers.

(d) The residual stream \(X\) grows as sub-layer outputs are added to it. LayerNorm re-centres and re-scales the copy that each \(F\) sees, so every sub-layer works on inputs of the same scale and its slopes \(A_k\) stay bounded at every depth. In the pre-LN layout the identity path itself never passes through a LayerNorm, so the highway stays clean. (In the original post-LN layout, \(Z = \operatorname{LN}(X + F(X))\), the identity path goes through a LayerNorm Jacobian at every sub-layer, which is one reason deep post-LN stacks need learning-rate warmup.)
